articles.full_text:
It turns out the end of summer doesn’t mean the end of summer weather.
Much of Santa Barbara County will have another long heat wave starting Friday and lasting through next week, said Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office.
“It’s going to stay hot through the middle part of October,” Kittell said.
The agency issued an Extreme Heat Watch for Santa Barbara, Goleta, other South Coast communities, and the Cuyama Valley — from 10 a.m. Friday through 8 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 8.
And the heat will likely last longer, Kittell said, but that’s as far out as the forecasts go.
It could be the longest heat wave we’ve had this season, he said, although the humidity and warm overnight temperatures may not be as bad as the last one.
Santa Maria and Lompoc may escape the worst of it, although they’re still going to have “concerning” hot weather.
Santa Barbara will see daytime high temperatures around 90 degrees and nighttime lows around 70 from Saturday through at least Tuesday, according to the latest forecast.
Goleta will be slightly cooler, with highs in the mid-80s.
The Santa Ynez Valley forecast has highs in the low-90s and lows around 60 starting this weekend.
The Santa Maria and Lompoc valleys will reach the mid- to high-80s, and then have nighttime lows around 60.
Overall, temperatures are expected up to 85 at the coast and up to 100 in the mountains and Cuyama Valley, the extreme heat watch says.
The low humidity and other conditions will cause a high risk for plume-dominated, fast-moving wildfires, according to meteorologists.
The region has a history of large fires in similar conditions, even though the weather likely will not trigger a Red Flag Warning, Kittell said.
“It will likely remain hot for the foreseeable future,” one presentation slide said, with a map showing huge red swaths designating above-normal temperatures across the western United States.
California may also have high tides and a small chance of rain from Hurricane Rachel, which will not make landfall in the state, according to the National Weather Service.
Drink plenty of cool, non-alcoholic beverages, especially those without sugar or caffeine. Do not wait until you are thirsty to drink. If you have fluid restrictions from your doctor, ask to see how much you should drink while the weather is hot.
Take care of those who might not be aware of high-temperature dangers or be able to react accordingly – especially the elderly, young children, and pets. Check on your neighbors.
Limit outdoor activity. Try to schedule outdoor activities during the cooler parts of the day, such as morning and evening hours. Be sure to wear sunscreen and rest often.
For those who work outside, be sure to take frequent rest breaks in a shaded area or air-conditioned room, if possible. Stay hydrated and take action by moving to a cooler space if you feel signs of heat exhaustion.
Take regular breaks in the shade or in an air-conditioned room. A few hours in air conditioning can help your body stay cooler. Taking a cool shower or bath can help too.
If you do not have air‐conditioning, consider arranging to spend at least parts of the day at another space that is cool. Electric fans may provide comfort, but when the temperature is in the high 90s, they will not prevent heat-related illness.
Wear appropriate clothing. Lightweight, light-colored, loose-fitting clothing works best.
Know the signs of heat exhaustion. If someone becomes dizzy, nauseated, or sweats heavily, find a cooler location for him or her immediately.
Know the signs of heat stroke. Heat stroke is much more serious than heat exhaustion. The symptoms are similar to heat exhaustion, but also include hot, flushed skin. With heat stroke, the person often stops sweating and the skin will be unusually dry. If heat stroke is a possibility, call 911 immediately. Heat stroke is life threatening!
Do not leave children (and pets) unattended in vehicles. It only takes a matter of minutes on a relatively mild day for a vehicle to reach deadly temperatures.
